GENERAL.label: Overall views, background and definitions
GENERAL.covers: Views on FDA's approach or on generative AI in healthcare as a whole (general support, hopes, worries or opposition), proposals that span several parts of the paper, such as a whole-lifecycle framework, and points about the paper's framing: its introduction, background, definitions of terms such as generative AI or foundation model, and which products count as devices (Sections I-III and VIII, which ask no numbered questions).
GENERAL.cues: support FDA's approach, too risky, promising, general worries about errors or hallucinations, definitions, scope
GENERAL.excludes: A specific proposal about one part of the paper goes to that part's code, even when it opens with a general remark. A worry about something the paper doesn't address, such as privacy or cost, even when stated as a general concern (MISC).

RISK.label: Assessing a device's risk
RISK.covers: How FDA should judge how risky a device is (Section IV, Questions 1-6). FDA proposes two axes: how independently the device acts, from giving neutral information, to directing what someone should do, to taking actions such as prescribing on its own; and how severe the harm would be if someone relied on a wrong output. Also covered: patient-facing versus clinician-facing use, generalist versus specialist users, risks that build up over a multi-turn conversation, and failing to escalate care or escalating it needlessly.
RISK.cues: risk framework, risk tiers, autonomy, severity of harm, patient-facing, escalation, triage, human in the loop
RISK.excludes: General warnings that AI is dangerous (GENERAL). How much evidence a device needs given its risk (PREMARKET). Systems that plan and carry out multi-step tasks with tools (AGENTIC).

PREMARKET.label: Evaluating a device before it is sold
PREMARKET.covers: What a device should demonstrate before FDA authorizes it (Section V, Questions 7-17). FDA proposes a competency-based approach with two parts: benchmarking, meaning large-scale testing of the finished device's knowledge, reasoning, safety behavior and communication across many inputs; and clinical confirmation, meaning evidence that it performs as intended in real or realistic clinical use. Also covered: scaling evidence to the device's risk, statistics, synthetic test data, comparators and acceptance criteria for open-ended outputs, comparison with care without the device, independent third-party testing, and other model architectures.
PREMARKET.cues: benchmark, validation, test set, red-teaming, clinical study, performance metrics, acceptance threshold, synthetic data, independent lab, before clearance
PREMARKET.excludes: Re-testing after the device is on the market, for example after an update (POSTMARKET). Testing specific to agentic systems (AGENTIC).

POSTMARKET.label: Oversight once a device is in use
POSTMARKET.covers: How devices are watched and changed after they reach the market (Section VI, Questions 18-24). Monitoring: tracking real-world performance, drift and errors, audit trails, whether AI supervisory agents could do some of the monitoring, and accepting more uncertainty before sale in return for stronger monitoring after. Shared responsibility: the roles of manufacturers, clinicians, hospitals, payers and others in monitoring and reporting. Changes: software updates, retraining, models that keep learning, how much evidence each change needs, predetermined change control plans (PCCPs), and changes made by a third-party foundation model's developer.
POSTMARKET.cues: postmarket, real-world performance, drift, monitoring, audit, adverse event reporting, update, retraining, version, PCCP, change control
POSTMARKET.excludes: A clinician monitoring a patient, which is care, not device oversight. The voluntary master file program (MASTER_FILES).

MASTER_FILES.label: Foundation model master files
MASTER_FILES.covers: FDA's idea of voluntary Foundation Model Master Files (Section VII.A, Question 25): the developer of a foundation model would confidentially give FDA information about it, such as a model card, known limitations, evaluation results and update commitments, which device makers could reference, with the developer's permission, in their own submissions.
MASTER_FILES.cues: master file, MAF, model card, system card, foundation model developer, confidential
MASTER_FILES.excludes: How a device maker should handle a third-party model's updates after launch (POSTMARKET).

AGENTIC.label: Agentic AI systems
AGENTIC.covers: Agentic AI (Section VII.B, Question 26): systems that plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, use external tools, or take a sequence of actions, for example in care coordination, documentation, patient outreach or workflow support; and how FDA should approach them, including which of these functions should count as devices.
AGENTIC.cues: agent, agentic, autonomous workflow, multi-step, tool use, orchestration
AGENTIC.excludes: The risk of a device taking a single action, such as prescribing (RISK). AI supervisory agents that monitor a device in use (POSTMARKET).

MISC.label: Outside the paper's topics
MISC.covers: A substantive point that fits none of the codes above, such as insurance or reimbursement, cost, workforce training, or a privacy or ethics concern not tied to any part of FDA's proposal. Its stance is always neutral, because it responds to nothing FDA proposed.
MISC.cues: insurance, reimbursement, cost, jobs, training of staff
MISC.excludes: A privacy or ethics point about a specific part of the proposal goes to that part's code.

skip.label: Skipped: no point of its own
skip.covers: Text that makes no point about the paper: greetings, thanks, introductions of the writer, disclaimers, signatures, contact details, and lead-ins that only announce a list of points to come.
skip.cues: thank you, sincerely, on behalf of, in my individual capacity, the following points
skip.excludes: Thanks or an introduction that also states a view, such as support for FDA's direction, gets a tag for that view (GENERAL). A heading that introduces a paragraph is not skipped: it is tagged together with that paragraph, as a range.

support.label: Supports FDA's approach
support.covers: Agrees with what FDA proposed on this point, as it stands.
support.cues: we support, agree, welcome, appropriately recognizes
support.excludes: Agreement that comes with requests for changes, additions or conditions (conditional).

conditional.label: Supports it with changes
conditional.covers: Accepts FDA's approach on this point but wants something added, changed, limited or clarified, including suggestions that extend what FDA proposed.
conditional.cues: should also, consider adding, provided that, however, we recommend
conditional.excludes: Rejecting the approach itself (oppose). Information that takes no position (neutral).

oppose.label: Opposes FDA's approach
oppose.covers: Disagrees with what FDA proposed on this point, or argues against the direction as a whole.
oppose.cues: should not, oppose, too risky, unnecessary, instead of
oppose.excludes: Wanting one part changed while accepting the rest (conditional).

neutral.label: Takes no position
neutral.covers: Information, examples or concerns that take no position on what FDA proposed, and every MISC point, which responds to nothing FDA proposed.
neutral.cues: for example, in our experience, I want to note
neutral.excludes: A concern offered as a reason to change FDA's approach (conditional) or to reject it (oppose), unless it is a MISC point.

GEN.label: Overall approach and general views
GEN.covers: Views on the paper or FDA's direction as a whole rather than on one question: overall support, concerns or opposition; regulatory philosophy (risk-based oversight, least burdensome principles, total product life cycle, balancing innovation with safety); whether, when and how FDA should move to guidance, rules, pilots or further engagement; legal-authority questions; consistency with existing FDA AI policies; international harmonization; comment-process requests such as extensions or public meetings.

Q1.label: Two-axis risk framework and additional dimensions
Q1.covers: Whether a risk framework built on two axes (how much the function acts or directs action, and how severe the harm is from relying on a wrong output) captures what matters for GenAI risk; whether and how to add dimensions such as reversibility of the resulting action, downstream safeguards, time pressure in the setting, or traceability of outputs to primary sources.

Q2.label: Directiveness spectrum for informational functions
Q2.covers: How to handle informational functions that range from non-directive to action-directing; which output features (wording, specificity, personalization, context) should raise or lower risk once intended use is accounted for; what would give manufacturers clarity and predictability given that directiveness is a continuum. Includes FDA's views that substance and context matter more than trigger words, that disclaimers such as 'talk to your doctor' may not make an output less directive, and that consequence severity moderates the risk of action-directing outputs.

Q9.label: Benchmarking structure and methods
Q9.covers: Whether the proposed benchmarking elements (safety, clinical proficiency, generalizability, agentic) would give adequate evidence of safety and effectiveness; missing, redundant or miscategorized elements; external standards that could be used. Also the general benchmarking principles: prespecified methods and acceptance criteria, scoring rubrics grounded in guidelines or expert input, independent adjudicators (including LLM adjudicators), enough clinical scope, datasets representative of deployment settings, and simulation, synthetic test generation or virtual patients. It also covers points about any single benchmarking element: safety-critical recognition and escalation; scope maintenance and boundary adherence; calibration, uncertainty and clinical deferral; clinical knowledge and task fidelity; information gathering and clinical analysis; quantitative and measurement analysis; communication quality and user comprehension; robustness, reliability and reproducibility; subgroup performance; agentic competencies.
